kernelIdea: If n ∤ m, then m = nk + r for some r with 1 ≤ r ≤ n−1 — so "not divisible" splits into n−1 cases. This makes proof by cases the standard tool for divisibility.

kernels.l1: Sharing among three, you have none, one, or two left over. Never more.
kernels.l2: When you share into groups, what is left over is always smaller than the number of groups. So there are only a few kinds of leftover to check.
kernels.l3: Every whole number can be written as a multiple of 3 plus a leftover of 0, 1, or 2. So there are only three kinds of number, and you can split into cases and check them all.
kernels.l4: If n ∤ m then m = nk + r with 1 ≤ r ≤ n−1, so "not divisible by n" splits into n−1 cases. Split into cases is therefore the standard tool for divisibility arguments.
kernels.l5: Dividing leaves a quotient and a remainder smaller than the divisor. That splits the integers into finitely many remainder classes, which is what makes case analysis exhaustive.
kernels.l6: Division with remainder splits the integers into finitely many remainder classes, which is what makes proof by cases a complete method.
kernels.l7: Division with remainder writes every integer as a multiple plus a remainder smaller than the divisor, splitting the integers into finitely many classes. Divisibility statements are therefore settled by finitely many cases.
kernels.l8: The division algorithm makes ℤ a Euclidean domain; the residue classes are the elements of ℤ/nℤ, and proof by cases is computation in that quotient ring.
